title: LAPA
subtitle: The first private airline to break the state monopoly. Then it broke itself.
summary: Lineas Aereas Privadas Argentinas began flying in May 1978 and by the mid-1990s held about 30% of Argentina's domestic market with a fleet of more than 30 aircraft. Flight 3142 crashed on takeoff from Aeroparque in August 1999 killing 65 people and exposing training and maintenance failures, and the airline filed for bankruptcy in 2001 before flying its last service in April 2003.
lesson: Growth bought with deregulated route access is only as durable as the safety culture underneath it.

title: The Argentine bullet train
subtitle: The contract was signed, the loans arranged, and then the credit market closed.
summary: Nestor Kirchner announced a 710 km line at 320 km/h linking Buenos Aires, Rosario and Cordoba in April 2006, budgeted at $4 billion with eight Alstom trainsets and $2 billion of French bank loans behind a turnkey contract signed in April 2008. Alstom placed the project on stand-by in February 2009 after the financial crisis, and in December 2012 the transport minister rejected high-speed rail outright, with no track ever laid.
lesson: A turnkey contract signed on foreign credit transfers no risk; when the lenders retreat, all you own is paper.
locationRole: Planned intermediate station on the corridor

title: The Trans-Amazonian Highway
subtitle: A road to march the nation inland. The forest took back the western third.
summary: Announced in June 1970 to run 4,977 km from Brazil's northeast toward Peru, the highway was cleared or partly paved to about 4,260 km by the mid-1970s, with 100-hectare plots and planned agrovilas for settlers every 10 km. Disease, seasonal flooding and unsuitable soils defeated the scheme: 48% of the first 1,187 allocated plots were abandoned within six years, and the western sections remain impassable for months each year.
lesson: An access road does not create an economy; establish whether the land can carry the settlement before you cut it.

title: The Xingu dam cascade
subtitle: A cascade of dams for one river, stopped by the people who lived on it.
summary: Eletronorte's 1979 master plan for the Xingu basin called for six dams totalling 24 GW with a flood zone of roughly 2 million hectares. More than 3,000 people, mainly Kayapo, Juruna and Arara, converged on Altamira in February 1989 to oppose it, and with the 1988 constitution and a World Bank withdrawal behind them Eletronorte abandoned five of the six sites.
lesson: Consent sought late behaves like a veto; a plan with no budget for the people on the land is not finished.

title: VASP
subtitle: The state built the airline. The buyer could not carry the losses.
summary: Founded by the state of Sao Paulo in 1933 and based at Congonhas, VASP grew into Brazil's second-largest carrier with a fleet of about 27 aircraft before being privatised in 1990 under Wagner Canhedo. Its market share fell to roughly 10%, the civil aviation authority grounded the airline on 27 January 2005, and a Sao Paulo court declared it bankrupt in September 2008.
lesson: Privatisation transfers the losses along with the assets; an owner without the state's balance sheet cannot absorb an ageing fleet.
locationRole: Headquarters and operating base at Congonhas

title: Lojas Mappin
subtitle: It taught Brazil to buy on instalments. The habit outlived the shop.
summary: Founded in 1913 and anchored on its Praca Ramos store, Mappin pioneered Brazilian department store retail, introducing the crediario instalment plan and the country's first in-store parking. It absorbed the Mesbla chain in 1996, could not manage the enlarged business, and closed in 1999, with stores looted in Campinas and elsewhere as the news spread.
lesson: An innovation competitors can copy for free is not a moat, and scale acquired in a hurry still has to be run.
locationRole: Flagship store in the city centre

title: The El Mutun steel contract
subtitle: One of the world's largest iron deposits, and no gas to smelt it with.
summary: In 2007 Jindal Steel and Power signed a $2.1 billion contract to work the El Mutun iron ore and build a 1.7 million tonne steel complex, conditional on Bolivia supplying 10 million cubic metres of gas a day plus land and access. Bolivia could not deliver, cashed $36 million of Jindal's performance bonds, and Jindal terminated the contract, winning $22.5 million back from an ICC tribunal in Paris in August 2014.
lesson: Confirm your counterparty can deliver its half before committing capital to a plant that only works if they do.
locationRole: Iron ore deposit and planned steel complex

title: The TIPNIS highway
subtitle: Bolivia's first indigenous president said the road would be built anyway. It was not.
summary: A 300 km highway through the Isiboro Secure indigenous territory was the centrepiece of Evo Morales's infrastructure agenda, with $330 million of the $415 million cost pledged by Brazil's BNDES. After police broke up a 500 km protest march near Yucumo in September 2011 and two ministers resigned, Morales cancelled the plan on 21 October 2011.
lesson: When the political cost of a project lands on the government's own base, no amount of financing will carry it through.
locationRole: Protected indigenous territory the road would have crossed

title: The Chirajara bridge
subtitle: Rebuilt ahead of schedule, and still nobody can drive across it.
summary: A 614 m cable-stayed bridge on the Bogota to Villavicencio highway partly collapsed during construction on 15 January 2018, killing about ten workers, and the remains were demolished that July. A redesigned 421 m replacement was completed in February 2024 but has never opened because the adjoining tunnels remain damaged, and the comptroller faulted the national infrastructure agency in August 2026 with service now projected for 2028.
lesson: A corridor is only as open as its worst link; finishing one structure early buys nothing if nobody sequences the rest.

title: HidroAysen
subtitle: Approved by the regulator, rejected by the country, cancelled by its own owners.
summary: Endesa and Colbun proposed five dams on the Baker and Pascua rivers in Patagonia, 2,750 MW for about $3.2 billion, and won environmental approval in May 2011 even though polling put 74% of Chileans against the scheme. A new administration formally rejected it in June 2014 and the partners cancelled in November 2017, writing off roughly $500 million already spent on studies and engineering.
lesson: An environmental permit is a political instrument with the lifespan of an administration, not a property right.
locationRole: Proposed dam sites on the Baker River

title: Home Depot Chile
subtitle: The playbook that built Atlanta did not know how Chileans build a house.
summary: Home Depot entered Chile in 1998 holding 66.67% of a joint venture with Falabella, expecting global purchasing scale and a standardised store format to overpower the incumbent Sodimac. Chilean buyers sourced materials through contractors and regional suppliers rather than American-style self-service aisles, Sodimac undercut it on landed cost, and Home Depot withdrew from the market in 2001.
lesson: Scale is not a moat in a market whose buying habits and supply chains you have not actually studied.

title: Metrolima
subtitle: The network was approved, drawn and costed. Nothing was ever dug.
summary: A Swedish consulting firm working with Peruvian planners designed a five-line underground network for Lima and Callao between 1972 and 1973, costed at US$317 million and formally approved by the government in 1974. Political instability after President Velasco's health crisis, the seismic engineering burden of the Lima basin and the mid-1970s financing crunch stopped the scheme at the design stage.
lesson: Approval is the cheapest milestone in a project; a plan that cannot survive one change of government was never funded.

title: Ferrocarriles del Ecuador
subtitle: A railway over the Andes, liquidated with the reserves almost empty.
summary: Ecuador's state railway ran about 965 km of track between Guayaquil and Quito across passes above 4,000 metres, with Chimbacalle station serving as the Quito terminus from 1908. Decree 1057 of 16 May 2020 ordered its liquidation after $144 million of accumulated losses, a workforce cut from 325 to 103 and $1,000 left in reserves, leaving roughly 25 km running as heritage tourism.
lesson: A subsidised service with no plan to stop being one is a slow liquidation; decide early what the asset is actually for.

title: Solucion Vial Guayasamin
subtitle: A tunnel to the valleys, voided from the moment it was signed.
summary: Quito contracted China Road and Bridges Corporation in 2016 for a $131 million tunnel and grade-separated corridor along Avenida Oswaldo Guayasamin, serving more than 200,000 daily commuters between the city and the Tumbaco and Cumbaya valleys. On 19 September 2025 an international arbitration tribunal ruled the contract absolutely null from its inception, sparing Quito a $40 million claim and ending the project.
lesson: Shortcuts in procurement do not speed a project up; they hand the other side a way to unwind the whole contract.
locationRole: Planned tunnel corridor to the eastern valleys

title: The Yacyreta reservoir
subtitle: The dam was finished. The people it displaced were not.
summary: Yacyreta could generate power by 1989, but the World Bank held its reservoir at 76 metres rather than the design level of 83 until the 40,000 to 70,000 people the full pool would displace had been resettled. By 1999 only 4,266 families had been moved into completed housing, and the reservoir was not raised until 25 February 2011, seventeen years behind schedule.
lesson: Mitigation you defer becomes the binding constraint; the cheapest moment to resettle people is before the concrete is poured.
locationRole: Binational dam and reservoir on the Parana

title: The Ferrocarril de Chiriqui
subtitle: It carried the province's coffee down the mountain until the highway did.
summary: Opened on 23 April 1916, the narrow-gauge line ran roughly 50 km from David up to Boquete, carrying Chiriqui's coffee and fruit and making David the province's operational and commercial hub. The Pan-American Highway took its traffic, services ceased around 1990 after 74 years, and the tracks were lifted in the early 2000s, leaving the David depot to be converted into a public library.
lesson: Infrastructure is judged on continued relevance, not on how long it lasted; a fixed route loses to one that reaches the door.

title: The Atlantic Railroad
subtitle: A century of coffee to the Caribbean, ended by one afternoon's earthquake.
summary: Begun under a revised concession in 1871 and completed on 7 December 1890 after Minor Keith financed the last stretch on banana profits, the line carried Costa Rican coffee from San Jose to the Caribbean at Limon for 101 years. A magnitude 7.6 earthquake on 22 April 1991 wrecked the track, including the crossing of the Pacuare River, and the government never repaired it.
lesson: Single-route infrastructure in a seismic zone needs its rebuilding plan written before the earthquake, not decided afterwards.

title: Trans 450
subtitle: Tegucigalpa built the stations and never bought the buses.
summary: Announced in November 2010, the bus rapid transit system drew about $50 to $58 million from the Inter-American Development Bank and others, and lanes and stations at Colonia Kennedy and Miraflores were built between 2011 and 2015. No fleet was ever procured, a transparency investigation opened in 2016, and Mayor Jorge Aldana cancelled the project on 20 September 2022, leaving a 1,450 million lempira debt running to about 2042.
lesson: Buy the part that carries passengers first; concrete without rolling stock is a debt with no revenue attached to it.
locationRole: Bus lanes and stations on the central corridor

title: Puente Papa Francisco
subtitle: The engineers said not to open it. The ribbon was cut anyway.
summary: Tegucigalpa built a 543 million lempira flyover on the Anillo Periferico and opened one bidirectional lane on 21 November 2025, ahead of the promised date. Cracks of 1.5 to 2 mm in the deck and columns widened within days, the bridge was closed on 19 January 2026, and municipal records released that July showed engineers had warned against opening and been pressed to authorise it.
lesson: A ribbon-cutting date is not an engineering milestone; when the schedule overrules the inspection, the defect is still there.

title: The La Union tuna port
subtitle: France paid for the port and the boats. The catch never came.
summary: France financed a $50 million tuna processing port at La Union, completed in 1981 together with two large seiners meant to supply it. The vessels landed meagre catches, the facility was languishing by 1985 without maintenance, and United States embargoes on Salvadoran tuna from 1986 under the Marine Mammal Protection Act closed the export market for good.
lesson: A vertically integrated plant is hostage to its weakest link, and to the trade rules of the market it was built to serve.

title: The Jamaica Railway
subtitle: Studied by Canada, India and China. Never once restarted.
summary: Jamaica built about 160 miles of railway from 1845, radiating from Kingston Railway Station to Montego Bay and the bauxite interior, until accumulated deficits and hurricane damage ended passenger and freight service in October 1992. Feasibility studies by Canadian National, Indian Railways and Chinese partners, a short-line trial that closed in August 2012 and a student service discontinued in January 2025 all failed to restore it.
lesson: Repeated feasibility studies are a substitute for a funding decision rather than a step towards one.
locationRole: Kingston terminus of the main line

title: Silicon Graphics
subtitle: It rendered Hollywood's dinosaurs. Commodity boxes rendered it obsolete.
summary: Founded in Mountain View in 1981, SGI dominated 3D visualisation and high-performance computing through the 1980s and 1990s from a campus at 1600 Amphitheatre Parkway. Successive bets on Intel's Itanium, on Linux IA-32 systems and on a late supercomputing repositioning all failed, and SGI filed for Chapter 11 in April 2009 with its assets sold to Rackable Systems that May.
lesson: A premium architecture loses to commodity parts unless you have decided in advance which layer you can still charge for.

title: Google Glass
subtitle: A camera on your face solved a problem nobody had, and created several.
summary: Unveiled at Google I/O in April 2012 and sold to Explorers from 2013 at $1,500, Glass managed four to eight hours of intermittent use or under an hour of continuous recording, and was banned from bars and theatres over its camera. The consumer programme ended on 15 January 2015, and the enterprise editions that replaced it were withdrawn from sale in March 2023 with support closing that September.
lesson: Bystanders are users too; a device that unsettles the people around it gets barred from the places it needs to work.

title: The T-Mobile Sidekick
subtitle: Everything lived in the cloud, until the cloud lost the backups.
summary: Danger Inc. built the cloud-native Hiptop, sold by T-Mobile as the Sidekick from 2002, and Microsoft bought the company for about $500 million in February 2008 without migrating its ageing Sun and Oracle infrastructure. A data centre failure on 2 October 2009 lost contacts, photos and messages for roughly 800,000 subscribers when the backup systems also failed, and the service was discontinued on 31 May 2011.
lesson: An untested backup is not a backup; when the product lives in your data centre, the data centre is the product.

title: Douglas Aircraft
subtitle: The order book was enormous. Every aircraft sold made the hole deeper.
summary: Douglas launched the DC-9 in 1963 and by 1966 held hundreds of orders against a backlog above $3 billion, but built each aircraft as a near-custom job while Boeing moved to modular production lines. Assembly costs overran by $27 million in fiscal 1966 alone, internal projections put the company a year from insolvency, and it was forced into a merger with McDonnell announced on 28 April 1967.
lesson: Demand can bankrupt you; if unit costs rise with volume, every additional order accelerates the failure.

title: Pan American World Airways
subtitle: It flew everywhere abroad and had nowhere at home to feed the planes.
summary: Founded in 1927, Pan Am built the first genuinely global route network and leased 613,000 square feet across fifteen floors of the Park Avenue tower that carried its name. Deregulation in 1978 left it without a domestic feeder network, Lockerbie and the Gulf War compounded the damage, and after Delta withdrew its support the airline shut down on 4 December 1991, ending about 11,000 jobs.
lesson: A business that depends on someone else's network to deliver its customers is one policy change from having none.

title: Tower Records
subtitle: The world's largest record store, in the year records stopped selling.
summary: Tower's Broadway and East Fourth Street store opened in 1983 as the self-declared world's largest record store, 25,000 square feet holding more than 100,000 titles. Parent company MTS filed for bankruptcy in 2003, the four major labels stopped shipping in August 2006 over unpaid invoices, and Great American Group bought the chain at auction that October and liquidated all 89 to 93 stores by December, ending about 3,000 jobs.
lesson: Comprehensive inventory stops being an advantage once distribution costs nothing; check whether the moat you defend still exists.
locationRole: Flagship store at Broadway and East Fourth Street

title: Vioxx
subtitle: A trial meant to widen the label found the reason to withdraw the drug.
summary: Merck ran the APPROVe trial from about 2000, giving 2,600 patients with a history of colorectal adenomas either rofecoxib or placebo for 156 weeks to win a polyp-prevention indication for a drug already selling $2.5 billion a year in over 80 countries. After 18 months the Vioxx arm showed confirmed cardiovascular events in 3.5% of patients against 1.9% on placebo, and Merck withdrew the drug worldwide in September 2004, later settling some 27,000 suits for $4.85 billion.
lesson: Late-emerging harm only shows up in long-horizon trials; a signal that needs eighteen months will never appear in a short study.
locationRole: Corporate headquarters where the withdrawal was announced

title: Westway
subtitle: A highway buried under a park, sunk by striped bass larvae.
summary: Proposed in 1969 and settled in form by 1974, Westway would have put a six-lane highway beneath forty acres of new landfill and parkland along Manhattan's west side for $2.1 billion, 90% federally funded. A disclosure in June 1984 showed consultants had concealed evidence of harm to Hudson striped bass larvae, the courts blocked the project under the Clean Water Act, and it was abandoned on 10 September 1985.
lesson: Concealing an adverse finding converts a manageable environmental problem into a fatal legal one.
locationRole: Hudson River waterfront the highway would have covered

title: Mirabel International Airport
subtitle: The land was seized, the airport built, the road and railway never came.
summary: Ottawa expropriated 97,000 acres from about 3,200 owners in March 1969 and opened Mirabel in 1975 at a cost near $500 million, roughly 50 km from Montreal, assuming highways and a rail link would follow. Neither arrived at the scale required, passengers drifted back to Dorval 22 km from downtown, scheduled passenger service ended in 2004 and the terminal was demolished in 2014 and 2015.
lesson: A site is worth only the access actually built to it; if the connection sits in someone else's budget, assume it will not arrive.

title: The Olympic Stadium roof
subtitle: A retractable roof that could not be moved in wind, and tore when it was.
summary: Roger Taillibert's retractable Kevlar roof for Montreal's 1976 Olympic stadium was not installed until April 1987, could not operate in winds above 25 km/h and needed about a week between movements. It was opened only 80 to 88 times in eleven years, tore repeatedly including a 120 metre rip in June 1991, and was abandoned in 1998 for a fixed roof that accumulated some 7,453 rips of its own.
lesson: Design for the duty cycle the building will actually face, not for the photograph taken on opening day.

title: The Lower Churchill proposals
subtitle: Thirty years of studies for a river whose power had nowhere to go.
summary: Newfoundland and Labrador spent $118 million between 1972 and 2003 on studies, negotiations and engineering for hydro development on the Lower Churchill, under four successive premiers. Every proposal died on the same fact, that power leaving Labrador must cross Quebec: purchase agreements with New York and New Hampshire utilities lapsed for want of transmission, Premier Peckford rejected Hydro-Quebec's 1984 offer within 72 hours, and active pursuit was suspended in 1998 with no megawatts built.
lesson: If one party controls the only route to market, the resource is theirs to price until you build another route.
locationRole: Proposed dam sites on the Churchill River
